PCI Express, or PCIe. It's a high-speed serial bus standard that connects expansion cards and peripherals to your motherboard. It has largely replaced the older parallel PCI bus, offering dramatically higher bandwidth and lower latency. Today, PCIe is the standard for graphics cards, NVMe SSDs, and advanced I/O adapters.

PCIe is a serial bus, which means data flows in one direction at a time and is encoded serially as a sequence of bits. This is different from legacy PCI which was parallel. The serial design allows higher clock rates and longer cable distances with lower latency.

The number of lanes determines how much bandwidth you have. PCIe lanes come in configurations: 1x, 4x, 8x, and 16x. A 16-lane connection at PCIe 4.0 speed offers 32 gigabytes per second. That's sufficient for graphics cards and fast storage. Lower lane counts like 1x or 4x serve slower devices.

PCIe has gone through several generations. PCIe 3.0 offers 16 gigabytes per second per 16-lane slot. Generation 4.0 doubles that to 32 gigabytes per second. Generation 5.0 reaches 64 gigabytes per second. Generation 6.0 goes even higher. Each new generation is backward-compatible with older cards, though at slower speeds.

The topology on your motherboard is hierarchical. A root complex integrated into the chipset manages a tree of PCIe switches and devices. Each slot gets a unique address, allowing the operating system to discover and communicate with each device independently.

Hot-swapping is supported in theory. You can remove and insert cards without rebooting. But driver support varies. Server and enterprise setups rely on this capability. Consumer boards are less thoroughly tested for hot-swapping.

Power delivery through PCIe is limited to 75 watts per slot for a 16-lane slot. High-power devices like GPUs need auxiliary power connectors running directly from the power supply. Low-power devices like SSDs and network cards draw all their power from the slot itself.

The PCIe controller on your motherboard's chipset implements the protocol layer and translates CPU requests into PCIe transactions. Its quality and driver support affect device stability.

Some motherboards support bifurcation—the ability to split one 16-lane slot into multiple 4-lane slots. This allows you to install multiple M.2 SSDs or other 4-lane devices in a single slot if your board supports it.
